newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan adopts action plan on sexual discrimination.
newsitem.headline: Japan adopts action plan on sexual discrimination.

text.p: Japan's cabinet on Friday approved an action plan designed to serve as the basis for policies to curb sexual harassment, sexual violence and practices which discriminate against women.

The action plan, compiled by a government panel headed by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, calls for the study of laws to prevent sexual harassment and for a review of Japan's toothless 1986 Equal Employment Opportunity Law.

The plan, to run until the year 2000, also calls for a review of the Labour Standard Law, which bans firms from making women work after 10 p.m., except for a handful of jobs such as doctors, nurses and broadcasters.
The cabinet decision follows the September 1995 U.N. conference on women in Beijing, which called on nations to establish action plans by the end of this year.

The release of the plan also follows a government agency report on sexual harassment on Thursday which said 92.5 percent of 239 firms surveyed during April and June had adopted no countermeasures, such as counsellors and outside or neutral complaint handlers, to deal with sexual harassment.
Of those firms without such countermeasures, 75 percent replied they felt they did not need to adopt such measures in the future, the Management and Coordination Agency said.
A 1995 survey by a major labour union showed 60 percent of female workers said they had experienced some form of sexual harassment at the workplace.

Hashimoto's action plan also takes aim at mass media and Internet images that demean women, including violent pornography and language which violates women's rights, and calls for concerted efforts to stamp out child pornography and child prostitution.
Rampant teenage prostitution through telephone dating services is singled out as a problem requiring legal measures.
The report calls for special temporary measures to realise the equality of opportunity between genders and increase women's participation in the national decision-making process.
Critics of the government's approach to discrimination have expressed doubt that plans to "review" laws or "study" problems would lead to concrete action.
They cite the Equal Employment Opportunity Law, passed with much fanfare, which included no legal enforcement provisions.
A government white paper on equality, released last March, said women were making advances in education and employment but still ran into a "glass ceiling" as they rose higher.
Even as women escaped a traditional homemaker role, they were burdened with housework on top of workplace demands, the report said.

"Roles are now viewed somewhat differently: 'A man's place is at work, and a woman's place is at work and in the home," the report said of the passing of the traditional view of the woman's place as in the home.
